findings.passage: Where Six strains is what he does when the threat actually arrives. A Six moves toward certainty: prepare, test the people in charge, plan for the worst, hold on. Fike moves away.
findings.problem: The discriminator is built against a phobic-Six stereotype. Counterphobic Six, which moves toward danger to master fear, is never named, though the evidence record's own alternative_case raises it and the article prints counterphobic-shaped material: "I wanted there to be some sort of danger" (used as Seven evidence), knocking down an officer he thought had a gun ("Immediately my instinct, boom"), the apple tattoo as a sign aimed at older white men who treated him badly, and "all the way there without dying." The same stereotype recurs in the triad primer ("A Six handles fear by bracing for it") and the FAQ ("A Six braces, prepares and tests the people in charge"). The similarity advisory tripped on that primer against Florence Pugh's profile ("handles fear by") and near-matches Dylan Patel's and Kareem Rahma's Seven diagnosis lines. The vocabulary alone is ordinary, but compared argument to argument, the three-type "X handles fear by..." primer is reusable scaffolding that could sit in any Seven profile, and here it carries the stereotype into the type answer.
findings.acceptance_test: The Six section names the counterphobic variant and tests it against at least one specific observation (for example, whether his danger-seeking is told as wonder and escape, "Alice in Wonderland", "another place", "like we'd traveled through time", or as confronting and testing a threat), and concedes what counterphobia or protectiveness explains (the officer incident, the tattoo defiance). Body, FAQ and triad paragraph no longer define Six only as bracing, preparing and testing authority. The triad primer is cut to one sentence or replaced with Fike-specific content, without the "handles fear by" template.

findings.passage: The plainest statement of the pattern in his own words comes from the same Zane Lowe film:
findings.problem: The codependency line is presented as the plainest statement of the Seven escape pattern, but in the film it is framed as support-seeking. Immediately before it (Lowe film, about 24:20-24:35 in the cached captions) he says "I want like a mentor though... an older mentor... someone that's been through a little bit of this." Near the end (about 47:45-47:58) he returns to it: "that is my idea of stability and it's always in another person so maybe I need to rethink that... that codependency we talked about." Locating stability in a guide or partner is the Six's core strategy. The Six section also omits his standing arrangement with his manager Reed Bennett, an external check on himself: "if I ever try to convince you otherwise, it's a lie. Don't listen to me. I'm manipulative!" (Evening Standard, July 2023). Only the "anywhere else but in my body" half of the passage is distinctly Seven. The article recasts the most Six-diagnostic material in the record as Seven evidence and keeps it out of the Six hearing.
findings.acceptance_test: The codependency section either drops "plainest statement of the pattern" or separates what is Seven in it (escaping being alone with himself) from what is Six (stability located in another person, a wished-for older mentor). The Six section includes the mentor and "stability... always in another person" lines, wording verified on audio because the 47:50 line is auto-caption only, plus the manager arrangement, and explains why they do not flip the read.

findings.passage: He signed a five-year contract on "Brother, got you."
findings.problem: This is one of three items offered as proof that Fike trusts where a Six would test authority (body and FAQ "Why isn't Dominic Fike a Type 6?"). The Armchair audio (about 01:02:14-01:02:45) shows the reverse direction. Levinson acknowledges Fike's drug problems, offers help ("We can get someone to help you, but you have to do this") and asks for a guarantee: "I need to know that you're not going to like fuck me on this." "Brother, got you" is Fike's pledge of reliability to the authority who was testing him. "Not understanding the stakes" refers to the show's scale ("when you see that budget... 20 semis"), not to an unexamined contract ("It's just a formality"). A loyalty pledge to a benefactor who offers support fits Six at least as well as Seven, so it cannot discriminate between them.
findings.acceptance_test: The handshake is removed from the Six-versus-Seven discriminator in the body and from the "Why isn't Dominic Fike a Type 6?" FAQ, or is described accurately (he promised Levinson reliability without grasping the show's scale) and no longer cited as evidence that he does not test people in charge. If the discriminator list needs a third item, it is replaced with an observation that actually separates 6 from 7.

findings.passage: That persistence is what tips the read to Seven.
findings.problem: The article rightly sets its own test: escape must persist when circumstances change, or addiction and trauma explain it. The support offered for sober-period persistence is thin. One piece is the motel exit, a scene the article itself says "Almost anyone would want out of." The other is "the interviews of 2025 and 2026", whose escape content is mostly retrospective narration of the using years. The April 2026 music line opens "When I was super bummy it was a good place to hide like in studios" and runs straight into the failed coke test and finishing a song before jail (Pigeons & Planes 2026, about 01:53-02:30). The draft introduces it in the present tense ("Music works the same way for him"). The band-aid and "I had a good time in jail" also describe 2017-2022. What does persist into 2025-2026 is the light retelling itself ("a good time in jail", "Cocaine's awesome. Sobriety's awesome"). That is genuine Seven evidence, but it is also the comic, promotional register the article flags. Meanwhile the dated 2026 behavior runs the other way: "I just don't party like that right now", staying out of people's faces, and property, friends and reputation goals for his son.
findings.acceptance_test: The text says precisely what persists into sober stretches: the reframing in the telling plus the motel exit. The motel's sober-stretch status can rest on his statements in the same film about trying to be sober and touring sober. Retrospective accounts are distinguished from current behavior, and "Music works the same way for him" is dated to the house-arrest years. "That persistence is what tips the read" is either backed by a sober-period behavioral instance beyond the motel or softened to match what the record shows.

findings.passage: The test is still ahead. In a settled, sober stretch, when he talks about what steadies him, does he credit people, preparation and stability he can count on (Six), or new projects, motion and keeping it light (Seven)?
findings.problem: The record already holds his answers to this exact question, and they lean Six. In July 2023, in the Lowe film the article treats as a sober stretch, he said "that is my idea of stability and it's always in another person." In April 2026, fatherhood makes him want to be "stable and sober", to "acquire property" and to "stay close to my friends", which the article itself calls "security goals, and Six gains ground here." Calling the test "still ahead" hides the fact that, on the article's own criterion, current evidence favors the alternative. The framing just before it ("a Seven doing the work Sevens grow by, staying with one thing long enough to finish it") is a soft growth-line rescue, and the album it describes was made "in real time on the road."
findings.acceptance_test: The closing either says plainly that the existing answers to its own test lean Six and states what keeps Seven in the lead (cross-year reframing such as the jail list; appetite for experience, as in "I want all of it"; fresh-start language such as "You're a baby again" and "refresh your whole friend group"), or replaces the test with one the record has not already answered that genuinely separates 6 from 7. The type answer and FAQ stay consistent with medium confidence.

findings.passage: It fits a watchful Six or Nine better.
findings.problem: The article says the only family testimony fits Nine better than Seven, then never tests Nine. The article prints a Nine-shaped cluster: "the most passive, quiet child... the observer"; "I've never been the type of guy to intrude on anybody's shit"; waiting for collaborators and women to make the first move; and music as a place "to hide" and "to not think about shit." That last line is numbing, Nine's signature move as much as Seven's, yet the article uses it as Seven evidence and against Four. Journalists also describe "no sense of drama." The research record sets Nine aside on appetite for intensity ("I want all of it", "all the way there without dying", "ride this out until the wheels fall off"). That argument is not in print, and much of the intensity evidence comes from using periods, the same confound the article applies to Seven's escape.
findings.acceptance_test: The rivals section gives Nine at least two sentences: what it explains (the quiet child, non-intrusion, numbing) and the specific observation that sets it aside, noting if that observation is drug-era. The "to not think about shit" line is no longer used as Seven-specific or anti-Four evidence without acknowledging that Nine shares it.

findings.passage: Type 3 fits the hunger for fame, but Threes protect the image, and he volunteers the failures, as with the shrooms audition:
findings.problem: The Three dismissal rests on a stereotype. In his genre, a self-deprecating failure told as comedy is itself a cool image, and the article notes elsewhere that his tattoo stories shift "with the room." It also leaves out Three-relevant self-report from the Interview conversation it already quotes: "I have the metrics... I get to observe people and where their interests are, which helps me decide how to build a track list," and the line it prints only as growth: "Back in 2019, when I got a deal, I was only thinking about what other people wanted." The article already holds better discriminators against Three: Godwin's "he defies any urge to shape it into a narrative of redemption," and his October 2026 pull-back from exposure ("you don't want to be in people's faces too much") during his first top-10 run.
findings.acceptance_test: The Three sentence acknowledges the audience-orientation material (metrics, "what other people wanted") and rests the dismissal on a discriminating observation, such as refusing the redemption arc or pulling back from exposure at a commercial peak, rather than on "volunteers the failures."

findings.passage: The Enneagram word for this is reframing. His word is a Transformers band-aid.
findings.problem: In his metaphor the band-aid is "all this money": success covering the wound. He was answering Shepard's question about why a functioning addict whose "act is working" would see anything as broken. That is substitution by success, a recovery insight any successful addict could voice, and a Three's achievement-covers-the-wound reading fits it as well. The line before it overclaims too: "the best description of the Seven defense in the record." Labeling it "reframing" turns a fit into apparent discrimination. The quote itself is excellent and should stay.
findings.acceptance_test: The gloss names what the band-aid is (money and success masking the need to heal), presents it as consistent with the Seven reading rather than as the record's clearest Seven-specific evidence, and uses an accurate term or no jargon.

protected_passages.passage: Ask him about it in different years and you get different jails:
protected_passages.reason: The dated three-telling list is the strongest Seven-specific evidence in the article: reframing shown across years and outlets, with the bad version ("It sucks, dude") kept in view rather than hidden.

protected_passages.passage: That is a fair reading, and it is about trauma, which can push a person of any type toward thrills. The question for a type argument is whether the same move shows up when the circumstances change.
protected_passages.reason: Gives the trauma alternative a fair hearing and states the right test for a type claim. Findings F4 and F5 ask the article to meet this test more precisely, not to drop it.

protected_passages.passage: A kid from a house like that could have gone looking for quiet. He went looking for a story.
protected_passages.reason: A specific, earned observation that makes the motive concrete without claiming interior access.

protected_passages.passage: That last line matters. A redemption story is a finished product, built to be admired, and he does not build one.
protected_passages.reason: A real discriminator against Three, drawn from independent testimony. It is better than the rivals-section sentence and should anchor the Three dismissal.

protected_passages.passage: The usual picture of a Seven is the one who makes the first call. He waits for it.
protected_passages.reason: Honest counterevidence the type does not neatly explain; it keeps the portrait from becoming a stereotyped Seven.

assessment: Type 7 at medium confidence is defensible. The most Seven-specific evidence is the cross-year reframing (the three jails, "Cocaine's awesome. Sobriety's awesome", relapses as "all good"), the appetite for experience ("I want all of it", the fucked-up knees), fresh-start and novelty language (Avalon as "another place", treatment as "a baby again") and three journalists' independent observations. The discriminator the article actually prints is weaker than that evidence. It argues against a phobic-Six stereotype and never names the counterphobic Six the record invites (F1). It misreads "Brother, got you", a loyalty pledge to an authority who was testing him (F2 context, F3). It recasts the most Six-diagnostic lines as Seven and keeps them out of the Six hearing: wanting an older mentor, stability "always in another person", the manager as external check (F2). Its sober-period persistence claim leans on retrospective quotes presented as current (F4). Its closing settle signal is already answered, Six-ward, by the 2023 and 2026 record (F5). Nine is named as a better fit for the family testimony and then dropped (F6), and Three is set aside by stereotype (F7). Wing is correctly left unknown. The only convenient arrow-style move is the soft growth framing of 2026 (F5). None of this requires changing the leading type; the fixes use evidence already in the record. But once Six is described fully, the margin is narrow. I am escalating contested_typing to true: the article itself says Six "has real material" and that frightened Sixes run too, and its own settle criterion currently favors Six. If the edit lowers confidence to an open or insufficient-evidence posture or flips to 6, treat it as a major thesis change. Sources checked against cached copies, not by ear: Armchair Expert Whisper transcript (01:02:06-01:03:00, 00:37:52-00:38:38), Zane Lowe film captions (23:56-25:04, 47:24-48:04), Pigeons & Planes 2026 transcript (01:12-02:40), Evening Standard 2023 and Interview 2026 cached pages. The 47:50 stability line is auto-caption only.
